items.title: Market research said the Walkman would fail
items.claim: Sony launched the TPS-L2 Walkman in 1979. What did market research suggest beforehand?

options.text: Strong demand from young consumers — supporting the launch
Likely failure: consumers reported they wanted recording capability, not just playback, and disliked the absence of speakers
No research was conducted because Akio Morita had no money for it

items.reveal:
Co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted a portable player so he could listen to opera on long flights. Akio Morita, despite hostile focus group findings, championed the launch. Sony hedged by initially offering it with two headphone jacks (so you could share) and a 'hotline' button to talk to a companion — both later dropped.

First-month sales in Japan were 30,000 units. By the early 1980s the Walkman was a global phenomenon and 'walkman' became a generic word for portable cassette player.

Clayton Christensen later used the case in 'The Innovator's Dilemma' to argue that existing customer research can't reliably predict demand for genuinely new products.
items.why: Market research has methodological limits. Consumers can tell you what they want among options they already know; they're worse at imagining a category that doesn't exist.

items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: ROCE compares like with like across firm sizes
items.claim: A firm has operating profit of £2 million, total assets of £15 million and current liabilities of £5 million. What is ROCE?
items.reveal_title: Operating profit divided by capital employed
items.reveal:
Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = £15m - £5m = £10m. ROCE = £2m / £10m = 20%.

ROCE is the most commonly cited single profitability measure in UK A-level. It is benchmarked against the cost of capital — if a firm consistently earns less than its weighted cost of capital, it is destroying shareholder value. UK FTSE 100 firms have averaged 10-15% ROCE over the last decade.
items.why: Absolute profit figures don't tell you whether capital was well used. A £2m profit from £10m of capital is 20%; the same profit from £100m of capital is 2%.
